row.name: Ksar el Kaoua
row.description: Ksar el Kaoua is a Roman castle situated in the ancient Roman province of Mauritania Caesarea [1] [2]. The site, located approximately 12 kilometers north of Ammi Moussa in the Wilaya of Relizane in western Algeria, is also known as the Ruins of the Latifundium of Kaoua [2]. This structure represents a large agricultural estate (latifundium) within the Late Roman Empire period in North Africa [1] [2].

row.name: Maumbury Rings
row.description: Maumbury Rings is a Neolithic henge in the south of Dorchester town in Dorset, England [1]. It is a large circular earthwork, 85 metres in diameter, with a single bank and an entrance to the north east [1]. Maumbury Rings were excavated by Harold St George Gray from 1908–1913 [1]. The excavations showed that the site originated in the later Neolithic period [1]. The excavations revealed an internal ditch which comprised a series of deep shafts cut into the chalk [1]. These number up to 45, and were up to 11 metres deep [1]. Maumbury Rings was remodelled in the Roman period when it was adapted for use as an amphitheatre for the use of the citizens of the nearby Roman town of Durnovaria (Dorchester) [1]. The site was used as an artillery fort by Parliament supporters in order to guard the southern approach to Dorchester [1].

row.name: Pacbitun
row.description: Pacbitun is a Maya archaeological site located near the town of San Ignacio in the Cayo District of west central Belize [1]. The site, at about 240 m above sea level, is one of the earliest known from the southern Maya Lowlands, and was inhabited for almost 2000 years, from ca. 900 BCE to 900 CE [1]. The central part of the site lies atop a partly artificial, east-west acropolis of limestone, and is marked today by over 40 masonry structures surrounding five major plazas [1]. First reported in the 1970s, Pacbitun was excavated extensively in the late 20th century by archaeologist Paul F. Healy and, in the early 21st century, by Terry G. Powis [1]. Based on these multi-year investigations, it is evident that the site was inhabited very early in Maya history, and flourished during the Late and Terminal Classic period (550-900 CE) [1]. Pacbitun was abandoned by about 900 CE, for reasons that remain unclear, but which surely were connected to the widespread abandonment of dozens of other, major centers of the Southern Lowlands at this time, as part of a phenomenon known as the Classic Maya collapse [1].

row.name: Tsagaan Salaa Rock Paintings
row.description: The Tsagaan Salaa rock paintings comprise one of the largest rock art complexes in North and Central Asia [1]. Spanning roughly 15 square kilometres along the White River Valley, the site contains over 10,000 figures [2] [3] [4]. Imagery documents the transition from big-game hunting to pastoral herding and horse-dependent nomadism [3] [5]. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011 as part of the Petroglyphic Complexes of the Mongolian Altai [3] [5].

row.name: Roman Temple Temnin
row.description: A Roman-era nymphaeum in Temnin el-Foka, located 28 km southwest of Baalbek in Lebanon's Bekaa Valley at 1,100 m elevation [1]. The arched watercourse is built of large stones, constructed 4 metres deep into a hillside, leading to an underground cistern [1]. A boundary pillar carved with the image of a goddess marks the outflow [1].

row.name: Catholme Ceremonial Complex
row.description: The Catholme ceremonial complex is an archaeological site of the Neolithic period in Staffordshire, England, near Barton-under-Needwood [1]. The site is near the River Trent to the east [1]. The features are not visible at ground level, but are visible as cropmarks seen in aerial photographs [1]. The site was investigated by Birmingham Archaeology from 2002 to 2004, involving a geophysical survey, Lidar and excavation [1]. The sequence in which the features were built has been suggested [1].

row.name: Sisira Well
row.description: The Sisira Well is an ancient well carved out of sandstone, located north of Sakaka near Zabal Castle in the Al-Jawf region of Saudi Arabia [1]. Underground tunnels and rock-carved channels once supplied surrounding farmland [1]. The well's name derives from the Canaanite military commander Sisera mentioned in the Hebrew Bible [1] [2].

row.name: Goosehill Camp
row.description: Goosehill Camp is a prehistoric earthwork that dates back to the Iron Age [1]. It consists of two concentric banks and ditches [1]. Goosehill Camp is within the Kingley Vale National Nature Reserve, on the South Downs [1]. Goosehill Camp's first recorded excavation was carried out by J. R. Boyden [1]. This excavation was carried out between 1953 and 1955 [1]. An excavation took place between 2008-2009 and was carried out by the University College London's Institute of Archaeology, under Mark Roberts [1]. These excavations were complemented by a topographical survey and a magnetometry survey [1].

row.name: Runkuraqay
row.description: Runkuraqay or Runku Raqay is an archaeological site on a mountain of the same name in Peru located in the Cusco Region, Urubamba Province, Machupicchu District [1]. It is situated southeast of the archaeological site Machu Picchu and south of the Vilcanota river [1]. The ruins lie on the southern slope of the mountain Runkuraqay near the Runkuraqay pass, northeast of the archaeological site Sayacmarca and southeast of the site Qunchamarka [1]. Hiram Bingham III visited the site in April 1915 [1]. Paul Fejos visited in 1940 [1].

row.name: Menhir of Meada
row.description: The Menhir of Meada is believed to be the largest menhir in the Iberian Peninsula that was entirely carved by humans [1]. It is situated 12 km to the north of Castelo de Vide in the Portalegre District of Portugal and is within the protected area of the Serra de São Mamede Natural Park [1]. The monolith, consisting of coarse-grained porphyroid granite, was discovered in a rural area, now used mainly for cork production, in 1965 [1]. Discovered in two pieces, it was restored in the 1990s, when the two parts were joined and the complete stone was replaced in its original location [1]. The menhir's total length is about 7.5 metres, with a maximum diameter of 1.25 metres and a circumference of 3.9 metres at the base [1]. It weighs around 18 tons [1]. Based on radiocarbon dating of coals discovered underneath the base, the menhir is believed to have been raised around 5000 BCE, in the Neo-Chalcolithic period, approximately the same time as the Coureleiros dolmens, or megalithic tombs, that are found in the same district [1].

row.name: Lligwy Burial Chamber
row.description: Lligwy Burial Chamber is a Neolithic burial chamber in Lligwy, near the east coast of Anglesey, Wales [1]. It consists of a circle of upright stones, made into a low chamber by a very large roof slab estimated at 25 tonnes [1]. Excavation in 1909 found the remains of some 15 to 30 people, and pottery suggesting a Late Neolithic date [1]. The eight uprights which support the massive capstone are larger than they at first appear, because half of their 2 m height is buried in the ground [1]. The capstone is about 5.5 m long and 4.5 m wide, with a thickness of around 1 m [1]. It is estimated to weigh about 25 tonnes and is in contact with only three of the uprights [1].

row.name: Welbeck Hill
row.description: Welbeck Hill is the site of Roman and early Saxon pottery finds, and an Anglo-Saxon cemetery, located around 1.75 miles from Laceby, and around 3 miles from Riby, in North East Lincolnshire [1]. Excavations on the southern slope of Welbeck Hill led to finds of a Roman 'grey ware dish and lug handle, also heavy well-fired shards and a cooking pot with a flat topped rim' [1]. Excavations of the Anglo-Saxon cemetery were begun by G. Taylor in 1962 after ploughing disturbed remains [1]. Three burial areas, dating from around the mid-5th and 6th centuries, have since been identified; north/south along the hill crest, east/west on the hill's western slope and a deposit of cremations on the eastern slope [1]. From 1962 to July 1976, 76 graves and 5 cremations were recorded [1].

row.name: Al Farid - The Lonely Castle
row.description: Qasr al-Farid ("The Lonely Castle") is an unfinished Nabataean tomb at Hegra (Mada'in Salih), a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Al-Ula, Saudi Arabia [1] [2]. It is the largest tomb at the site and uniquely features four large pilasters on its facade [3] [4]. Carved from a single rock outcrop starting from the top down around the 1st century AD, its lower third remains rough and unfinished [1] [2] [3]. The site contains 111 monumental tombs in total, with 94 decorated facades [5] [6].

row.name: Mullu Q'awa
row.description: Mullu Q'awa is an archaeological site in Peru on a mountain of that name [1]. It is located in the Cusco Region, Espinar Province, Alto Pichigua District [1]. It lies near the village of Mullu Q'awa [1]. It is situated on top of the mountain at a height of about 4,000 m [1]. The site was declared a National Cultural Heritage by Resolution No. 954-2010- INC on April 27, 2010 [1].

row.name: Boleigh Fogou
row.description: Boleigh Fogou is an Iron Age underground dry-stone passage near St Buryan in Cornwall, considered one of the best-preserved fogous in the county [1] [2] [3]. Unusual for having more than one entrance, it features a main passage with classic dry-stone and lintel construction [1] [2]. Excavation yielded Iron Age pottery [1] [3].

row.name: Tepe Sardar
row.description: Tepe Sardar, also Tapa Sardar or Tepe-e-Sardar, is an ancient Buddhist monastery in Afghanistan [1]. It is located near Ghazni, and it dominates the Dasht-i Manara plain [1]. The site displays two major artistic phases, an Hellenistic phase during the 3rd to 6th century CE, followed by a Sinicized-Indian phase during the 7th to 9th century [1]. Tapa Sardar is the ruin of a large Buddhist stupa - monastery complex which is located four Kilometers southeast of the city of Ghazni  [1]. A votive inscription was found at the site, saying that the sanctuary was known in the past as the Kanika mahārāja vihāra, suggesting a foundation date during the period of the Kushan Empire, in the 2nd-3rd century CE, possibly at the time of Kanishka II or Kanishka III [1]. The sanctuary was first destroyed by a great fire in the 7th century, putting an end to the period of Gandharan art at the site [1]. The sanctuary was rebuilt and expanded in the 7th-8th century CE [1].

row.name: Lighthouse of Leptis Magna
row.description: The remains of an ancient lighthouse at the harbour of Leptis Magna, a major Phoenician and Roman city at the mouth of the Wadi Lebda in present-day Al-Khums, Libya [1] [2] [3]. Founded by Phoenicians as early as the 7th century BC, the city flourished under Roman Emperor Septimius Severus (born there in 145 AD), who expanded the harbour and constructed the multi-story lighthouse reaching approximately 35 metres in height [2] [4] [5] [6]. Leptis Magna is a UNESCO World Heritage Site with some of the best-preserved Roman ruins in the Mediterranean [1] [4].

row.name: Rock Carvings at Vingen
row.description: One of the largest rock carving sites in Northern Europe, located along the Froysjoen strait in Bremanger, Vestland county, Norway [1]. The site contains approximately 2,300 documented figures, predominantly deer [1] [2]. First publicly documented in 1912 by Kristian Bing, though locals knew of the carvings since about 1884 [2] [3]. The motifs may represent fertility symbolism or concepts of life, death and reincarnation [4] [5]. Closed to the public by the Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage due to conservation concerns [1] [2].

row.name: Mandbjerghøj
row.description: The Mandbjerghøj is located next to the road through Øster Velling Skov forest, north of Øster Velling, west of Randers in Jutland [1]. Here there are two small granite boulders with engraved geometric patterns from the Bronze Age [1]. The two stones with petroglyphs stand some fifty metres from their original find spot [1]. There are also the almost completely destroyed remains of the Mandbjerghøj tumulus where the first stone with petroglyphs, which was part of the tumulus fence, was found in 1857 [1]. The tumulus which is now barely visible was originally about 24 m in diameter and four metres high [1]. In the middle of the mound was a typical male grave of the early Bronze Age (c. 1500 BC) [1]. In the grave a bronze sword and a gilt belt-hook were found, which bore the same motif as the rock carvings, thereby demonstrating that the tumulus and the carvings were made at the same date [1]. The stones depict concentric rings and three ovals, which themselves enclose two rings [1].

row.name: Tumamoc Hill
row.description: Tumamoc Hill is a butte located immediately west of "A" Mountain and downtown Tucson [1]. Tumamoc was a home to the ancient Hohokam people [1]. It is the site of the earliest known trincheras village, consisting of 160 foundations of round stone structures, as well as large stone perimeter walls [1]. Over 460 petroglyphs and a prehistoric garden beside the hill provide further evidence of Tumamoc’s importance to these people [1].

row.name: Archaeological Site of Dodoni
row.description: Oldest oracle in Greece, located 22 km southwest of Ioannina in Epirus, where priests called the Selloi interpreted the rustling of a sacred oak tree to deliver the prophecies of Zeus [1] [2] [3]. Lead question-tablets have been recovered, dating from the 6th to 2nd centuries BC [4]. King Pyrrhus of Epirus made Dodona his religious capital around 290 BC, grandly rebuilding the Temple of Zeus and constructing a 17,000-seat theatre that remains well preserved today [1] [2] [5]. The Naia festival held here featured athletic and dramatic contests [5]. The oracle ceased in the 4th century AD under Theodosius [1] [5].

row.name: Kinal
row.description: Kinal is a major pre-Columbian Maya archaeological site in the Petén Department of northern Guatemala [1]. The site's major occupational phase dates to the Late Classic period (600-900 AD), with evidence of a substantial expansionary building program during the first half of the 8th century AD [1]. The architectural style corresponds to the Late Classic period [1]. Kinal was discovered in the 1960s by archaeologist Ian Graham during a regional survey, though no excavations were conducted at that time [1] [2].

row.name: Brown Clee Hill
row.description: Brown Clee Hill is the highest hill in the rural English county of Shropshire [1]. Several Iron Age hill forts are dotted around the Clee Hills [1]. Nordy Bank is the last 'intact' survivor of three hill forts on Brown Clee [1]. The other two, at Abdon Burf and Clee Burf, have been largely lost to quarrying activity [1]. Nordy Bank occupies a sloping ridge top site and its ramparts are up to three metres high [1]. It was built some time in the British Iron Age first millennium BC and gives a commanding view of the local countryside [1].

row.name: Bedd Arthur
row.description: Bedd Arthur consists of a barely visible oval bank and ditch, with thirteen standing stones, none higher than 60 centimetres arranged inside along with two further fallen stones [1]. The stone layout measures around 20 by 10 metres [1]. The shape is not well defined and is generally described as sub-rectangular but has been described as a rectangle, a horseshoe, an oval and a pointed ellipse [1]. The site has not been excavated and is absent from authoritative surveys [1]. The site is in Eglwyswrw community, and is a Scheduled monument with legal protection from disturbance and is within the Pembrokeshire Coast National Park [1].

row.name: Twin Column Tomb
row.description: The Twin Column Tomb (Korean: 쌍기둥무덤) is a two-chambered burial tomb dating from the Koguryo period, located in Nampo, North Korea [1]. Listed as a National Treasure of North Korea, it is notable for the painting on the north wall of the back chamber [1]. The tomb was discovered by Japanese during Japan's occupation of the Korean Peninsula [1].

row.name: Roman Dam of Belas
row.description: The Roman Dam of Belas is a 3rd-century Roman barrier constructed to serve the city of Olisipo, located in civil parish of Queluz e Belas, municipality of Sintra [1]. The dam was constructed in the 3rd century, although it is unclear when it was abandoned [1]. The ancient ruins of the dam are survived by a central segment some 15.5 metres long, 8 metres tall and 7 metres wide, and reinforced by three buttresses [1]. The reservoir created by the dam warehoused approximately 125 cubic metres of water [1]. The channel from the structure extends 1,300 metres and is visible as it still intersects the more modern Águas Livres Aqueduct that was built over the old structures [1].

row.name: Macedonian Tower
row.description: The Macedonian Tower in Edirne, Turkey, is the sole surviving corner bastion of the Roman fortress built by Emperor Hadrian in the 2nd century AD when he founded the city as Hadrianopolis [1] [2] [3]. The rectangular castrum featured towers on all four corners [2] [3]. A wooden clock tower was built atop the Roman tower, later replaced in stone, but it was severely damaged by the 1953 earthquake and destroyed with dynamite that same year [2] [3].

row.name: Casma-Sechin Culture
row.description: The Casma–Sechin culture (c. 3600 BCE–200 BCE) of Peru refers to the large concentration of pre-historic ruins in the valleys of the Casma River and its tributary the Sechin River and along the nearby coast of the Pacific Ocean [1]. The ruins include major archaeological sites such as Sechin Bajo, Sechin Alto, Cerro Sechin, Mojeque, Chankillo, and Taukachi-Konkan, as well as other smaller sites [1]. Most of these inland sites are found in the river valleys about 20 kilometres distant from the ocean [1]. The seaside sites of Huaynuná and Las Haldas are found about 20 kilometres north and south of the mouth of the Casma River on the coast [1]. The area of the Casma/Sechin culture extended about 40 kilometres inland from the sea [1]. By 3000 BC, at a few locations in coastal Peru, including the Casma/Sechin valleys, a sizable population was present and undertaking large projects such as building pyramids and other ceremonial and monumental structures [1]. Radiocarbon dating indicates a plaza at Sechin Bajo was constructed in 3500 BCE [1].

row.name: Maiden Way
row.description: The Maiden Way or Maidenway was a roughly 20-mile Roman road in northern Britain connecting the Roman fort of Bravoniacum (Kirkby Thore) near Penrith with that of Magnis (Carvoran) on Hadrian's Wall, via the intermediate fort of Epiacum roughly half-way between the two [1]. Bravoniacum was a waypoint on the northern leg of the Roman road connecting Luguvalium (Carlisle) with Eboracum (York) and points south [1]. Magnis was one of the waypoints on the Stanegate beside Hadrian's Wall [1]. As such, the Maiden Way served as a shortcut for supplying the central and eastern areas of the Wall [1]. It also provided supplies to the lead and silver mines near Epiacum (Whitley Castle) [1]. Following the end of Roman rule in Britain, the Maiden Way was used as a drovers' road [1]. The route was probably named after the Maiden Castle fortlet guarding the Stainmore Pass to the east of the fort of Verterae [1].

row.name: Al Naslaa
row.description: The Al Naslaa rock is a landform 50 kilometres (31 mi) south of the Tayma oasis in Saudi Arabia [1]. It is a large sandstone rock split neatly down the middle into two parts, both balanced on small pedestals [1]. The overall shape of the rock is due to wind erosion and the chemical weathering made possible by the moist conditions in the protected underside of the rock [1]. It is split in two by a joint [1]. The rock is about 6 metres (20 ft) high and 9 metres (30 ft) wide, and is covered on its south-east face with numerous petroglyphs, including depictions of horses and ibex [1].

row.name: Sacul
row.description: Sacul is an archaeological site of the Maya civilization located in the upper drainage of the Mopan River, in the Petén department of Guatemala [1]. The city occupied an important trade route through the Maya Mountains [1]. The main period of occupation dates to the Late Classic Period [1]. In the late 8th century AD through to the early 9th century, Sacul was one of the few kingdoms in the southeastern Petén region to use its own Emblem Glyph, together with Ixtutz and Ucanal [1]. In AD 779 Sacul went to war against Ixkun and lost, but stelae at both cities record a visit to Ixkun by king Ch'iyel of Sacul just 11 years later and the two cities appear to have formed a military alliance at that time [1]. The site core is arranged around a number of plazas, one of which forms a monumental acropolis [1]. The site core includes pyramids, a ballcourt, a triadic complex and two E-Group astronomical complexes [1]. The last stela erected in Sacul bears a date corresponding to AD 800 [1].

row.name: Ta' Ġawhar Tower
row.description: Ta' Gawhar Tower is a round Punic-Roman tower in Safi, Malta [1] [2]. It is the best preserved of the six Punic-Roman towers in Malta, standing approximately seven wall courses high [1]. The tower was probably built during the Punic Wars and continued in use through the Roman period before its destruction in the 3rd century AD [1].

row.name: Medusa Mozaiği
row.description: The Medusa Mosaic is a floor mosaic in the odeon of the ancient city of Kibyra, in the Golhisar district of Burdur province, southwestern Turkey [1]. It depicts the mythological Medusa using the rare opus sectile technique with colorful marble pieces, making it one of the few surviving examples of this method worldwide [1] [2]. The odeon, unearthed in 2012 after three years of excavation, also served as the city's bouleterion (council house) [3] [4]. The mosaic is seasonally covered for winter protection and reopened each spring [1] [5]. Kibyra was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List in 2016 [4] [6].

row.name: Pañamarca
row.description: Panamarca is the southernmost monumental Moche site in Peru, constructed atop a granite hill in the lower Nepena Valley [1] [2]. The site features an imposing stepped adobe platform and is renowned for its vivid polychrome murals depicting priests, warriors, and supernatural beings [1] [2]. In 2024, researchers discovered a seventh-century throne room of a female ruler with painted adobe throne, the first such find in Moche archaeology [2] [3] [4].

row.name: Atsipades
row.description: Atsipades is an archaeological site of a Minoan peak sanctuary in western Crete [1]. The peak has its own specific name, Atsipades Korakias [1]. Atsipades Korakias is characterized by twin peaks [1]. The autumn equinox at Astipades can be seen between the peaks [1]. Votives, such as animal figurines, human figurines, and bowls, are often found in rock clefts at Astipades [1]. Atsipades is located above the village Atsipades, Agios Vasilios [1]. Atsipades was used for ancient Minoan religious rites [1].

row.name: Huacramarca
row.description: Huacramarca or Waqramarka (possibly from Quechua waqra horn, marka village) is an archaeological site on a mountain of the same name in Peru [1]. Huacramarca lies southeast of Contrahierbas, near the village Huallin (located in the Ancash Region, Asunción Province, Chacas District) [1]. The ruins are situated on top of the mountain Huacramarca at an elevation of 4,150 metres [1].

row.name: Ballygroll Prehistoric Landscape
row.description: Ballygroll Prehistoric Landscape is an 11-acre site in the townland of Ballygroll, County Londonderry [1]. It is a Scheduled Monument and a Monument in State Care [1]. The range and extent of the monuments is remarkable ranging in age from the Neolithic Period until the Late Bronze Age [1]. Most of the monuments on the site have not been fully excavated but it includes several cairns, alignments, standing stones, three different types of grave, a barrow, and a field wall system [1]. The area around the south and west flanks of Loughermore Mountain was first recorded as being an area with a significant number of ancient monuments in Ordnance Survey memoirs in 1835 [1]. However, many of these monuments have been damaged or destroyed [1].

row.name: Jach'a Phasa
row.description: Jach'a Phasa is an archaeological site in Bolivia located in the La Paz Department, Pacajes Province, Calacoto Municipality, about 2 km north-east of Rosario [1]. It is situated at a height of 4,126 metres on top of the mountain Jach'a Phasa north of the Mawri River [1]. The place is covered with more than 50 chullpa and surrounded by a wall [1]. The chullpa are constructed of stone of volcanic origin and mortar of mud and straw [1].

row.name: House of the Tiles
row.description: The House of the Tiles is a monumental Early Bronze Age building (two stories, approximately 12 x 25 m) located at the archaeological site of Lerna in southern Greece [1]. It is notable for several architectural features that were advanced for its time during the Helladic period, notably its roof covered by baked tiles, which gave the building its name [1]. The building belongs to the "corridor house" type [1]. The site was excavated during the early 1950s by the American School of Classical Studies under the direction of John Caskey of the University of Cincinnati [1]. The house had a stairway leading to a second story and was protected by a tiled roof; it also contained storage areas [1]. Debris found at the site contained thousands of terracotta tiles having fallen from the roof [1]. Although such roofs were also found in the Early Helladic site of Akovitika and later in the Mycenaean towns of Gla and Midea, they only became common in Greek architecture in the 7th century BC [1]. Carbon-14 dating indicates that the House of the Tiles was finally destroyed by fire in the 22nd century BC [1].

row.name: Quoyness Chambered Cairn
row.description: Quoyness chambered cairn is a Neolithic burial monument located on the island of Sanday in Orkney [1]. Similar to Maeshowe in design, the tomb was probably built around 3000 BC [1]. The skeletal remains of several people were uncovered in the tomb during excavation in 1867 [1]. The monument was partially restored and reconstructed after a second excavation during the early 1950s [1]. Quoyness chambered cairn is located on the Elsness peninsula [1]. The cairn sits on a wide, oval-shaped stone platform and was built with a mix of stones, earth and waste material intermixed with horizontal slabs [1]. A stone kerb surrounds the platform on the south and the west ends [1]. The cairn was excavated by James Farrer and George Petrie in 1867 [1].

row.name: British Block Cairn
row.description: The British Block Cairn is located on the Suffield Block in Alberta [1]. In the summers of 1961 and 1962, the Chief Superintendent of the Suffield Experimental Station, Mr. A. M. Pennie, granted crews from the Glenbow Foundation, consisting of R.G. Forbis, D. R. King, Frank O'Leary, Kenneth Smith, John Miller, and James Farmilo, access to the cairn [1]. Dating from around 1400 C.E, the site consists of a large boulder cairn surrounded by a ring of stones and a human effigy figure [1].

row.name: Laguna de las Momias
row.description: Laguna de las Momias (Lagoon of the Mummies), also known as Laguna de los Cóndores (Lagoon of the Condors) is an archaeological site located in Leimebamba, Chachapoyas province, in the Amazonas Region of Peru, excavated by the archaeologist Federico Kauffmann Doig [1]. Each funeral deposit contains a mummy in a seated position, wrapped in both flat and decorated textiles [1]. When excavating the Lagoon of the Mummies, there were six mausoleums found, each consisting of cube-shaped enclosures next to each other in a row [1]. The tombs were housed in caves with paintings on the walls related to the mausoleums and containing indecipherable symbols [1]. The enclosures were built with only three walls, the fourth being the rock wall [1]. In the tombs were various cultural objects, such as pottery, textiles, wood carvings the size of statues, clothing, silver, personal ornaments [1]. The mausoleums of the Lagoon of the Mummies were replete with funeral deposits, approximately two hundred; high-ranking individuals were buried there [1].

row.name: Ushiberd
row.description: Ushiberd (Armenian: Ուշիբերդ) is an Iron Age fortress located upon a hill just outside the village of Ushi in the Aragatsotn Province of Armenia [1]. It has almost completely collapsed except for portions of the walls that once surrounded the fortress, located around the edge of the hill before it descends [1]. Within the area that was once the interior of the fortress are large piles of large stones that once made up the fortification walls and structures within [1].

row.name: Rudna Glava
row.description: One of the earliest copper mines in Europe, dating to the 5th millennium BC in eastern Serbia [1]. Excavations by Borislav Jovanovic (1968-1986) uncovered mine shafts following veins of copper ore, some extending 15-20 metres into the hillside [2] [3] [4]. Miners used fire-setting and thermal shock techniques to fracture rock [3] [4]. Vincha culture pottery from the Gradac phase confirms the chronology [3] [4]. Added to Serbia's Archaeological Sites of Exceptional Importance in 1983 [1] [5].

row.name: Castlestrange Stone
row.description: The Castlestrange stone is located in the grounds of Castlestrange House near Athleague in County Roscommon, Ireland [1]. It is a granite boulder decorated with flowing spirals in the La Tène style, dating from the Iron Age period between 300 BC and 100 AD [1]. Only three other stones of this type have been found in Ireland, the Turoe Stone in County Galway, the Killycluggin Stone in County Cavan and the Derrykeighan Stone in County Antrim [1]. All four stones lie on roughly the same line connecting them on a map of Ireland [1].

row.name: Ennigaldi-Nanna's Museum
row.description: Ennigaldi-Nanna's museum is the earliest known public museum [1]. It dates to circa 530 BCE [1]. The curator was Ennigaldi, the daughter of Nabonidus, the last king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire [1]. It was in the state of Ur, in the modern-day Dhi Qar Governorate of Iraq, roughly 150 metres southeast of the famous Ziggurat of Ur [1]. The museum was discovered in 1925, when archaeologist Leonard Woolley excavated portions of the palace and temple complex at Ur [1]. He found dozens of artifacts, neatly arranged side by side, whose ages varied by centuries [1]. He determined that they were museum pieces, because they were accompanied by "museum labels"; clay drums written in three different languages, including Sumerian [1]. The artifacts came from the southern regions of Mesopotamia [1].

row.name: Tria Platania
row.description: During the construction work on the railway line Athens-Thessaloniki, the remains of an ancient farmhouse were discovered at Tria Platania [1]. Rescue excavations allowed a small part of the existing antiquities to be located and examined [1]. A study examined the remains of olives to determine how the olive oil was produced in the period from the fourth to the second century BC [1]. The place is located on the ancient road that connects the Thessalian province of Perraivia with the Macedonian province of Pieria, in the vicinity of the railway tunnel and the motorway exit Platamonas [1]. Most of the remains of the Tria Platania settlement were destroyed during the construction of the railway tunnel [1].

row.name: Sagalassos Archaeological Site
row.description: An ancient city in southwestern Turkey's Burdur Province, situated at 1,450-1,700m altitude in the Western Taurus Mountains [1] [2]. Sagalassos was conquered by Alexander the Great in 333 BC and became the 'first city of Pisidia' under Rome, reaching peak prosperity in the 2nd-3rd centuries AD [1] [3] [4]. The well-preserved ruins include a 9,000-seat theatre, monumental fountains, colossal baths, and colonnaded streets, with up to 90% of original building elements recoverable during excavations [3] [5] [6]. On the UNESCO Tentative List, it has been excavated since 1990 [6] [7].

row.name: Abbatija Tad-Dejr Hypogeal Complex
row.description: The Abbatija Tad-Dejr hypogeal complex is a paleochristian burial site in Rabat, Malta [1]. The early catacombs comprised a singular shaft and chamber tombs dug from the vertical face of a quarry [1]. Baldacchino tombs are often considered to be the richest out of the array of tomb types found in Maltese catacombs; at least three such tombs in this complex are heavily decorated with reliefs [1]. In the post-Roman period, the largest catacomb was enlarged and turned into a small church [1]. The presence in the hypogeum of a stone altar and the number of crosses carved into the rock surface suggest early Christian use [1]. A fresco that, until recently, decorated the apse over the supposed location of the original altar is now housed in the National Museum of Fine Arts [1]. The catacombs underwent various other phases of use, including as cow pens and for the quarrying of stone used in the production of lime [1]. The latter has resulted in extensive damage [1].

row.name: Brane Barrow
row.description: Brane Barrow, or Chapel Euny Barrow, is a Neolithic entrance grave located near the hamlet of Brane, Cornwall, England [1]. It is considered to be one of the smallest and best preserved burial monuments in Britain [1]. Brane Barrow is a scheduled burial monument located 317 yards south west of Brane End Farm, and 1.2 miles southwest of the village of Sancreed, in Cornwall [1]. The monument includes an entrance grave, situated in a low-lying pasture close to the upper Lamorna River [1]. The barrow is a circular mound of earth and stones, measuring up to 20 feet in diameter [1]. The mound is surrounded and retained by a border of large granite blocks [1]. It contains a rectangular stone-lined chamber measuring 7.5 ft long by 4 ft wide and 3 ft high [1]. The chamber is roofed with two capstones: a third capstone was removed at some point [1].

row.name: Khoit Tsenkher Cave Rock Art
row.description: Paleolithic cave paintings in Mankhan Sum, Khovd Province, Mongolia [1]. Painted images of stags, buffalo, ibex, lions, argali sheep, camels, elephants, and ostriches rendered in mineral-based rosy and brown pigments from walls to ceiling [1] [2]. Some animals overlap in palimpsest layers, and others are depicted with dots [1] [3].

row.name: Cusichaca River
row.description: The Cusichaca River valley in the Cusco Region is one of the most comprehensively studied archaeological areas in Peru, investigated since 1977 by Dr. Ann Kendall and the Cusichaca Trust [1] [2]. The valley contains Inca sites including Patallacta [1] [3] [4]. The archaeological data has been applied to restore approximately 30 km of canals and 600 ha of terracing to full productivity [5].

row.name: Chestnuts Long Barrow
row.description: Chestnuts Long Barrow, also known as Stony Warren or Long Warren, is a chambered long barrow near the village of Addington in the south-eastern English county of Kent [1]. The long barrow was built on land previously inhabited in the Mesolithic period [1]. It consisted of a sub-rectangular earthen tumulus, estimated to have been 15 metres in length, with a chamber built from sarsen megaliths on its eastern end [1]. Both inhumed and cremated human remains were placed within this chamber during the Neolithic period, representing at least nine or ten individuals [1]. These remains were found alongside pottery sherds, stone arrow heads, and a clay pendant [1]. In the 4th century AD, a Romano-British hut was erected next to the long barrow [1]. In the 12th or 13th century, the chamber was dug into and heavily damaged, either by treasure hunters or iconoclastic Christians [1]. The ruin attracted the interest of antiquarians in the 18th and 19th centuries, while archaeological excavation took place in 1957, followed by limited reconstruction [1].

row.name: Via Devana
row.description: The road linked major Roman military centres [1]. Its name derives from Chester's Latin name Deva, meaning "The Chester Road." Following the Roman withdrawal from Britain in 407 AD, the road fell into disuse and is now difficult to trace, especially in northern sections [1] [2]. The name "Via Devana" was coined in the 18th century by Charles Mason, a Cambridge scholar [1] [3].

row.name: Dolmen of Chianca
row.description: Discovered on 6 August 1909 by Francesco Samarelli and Angelo Mosso, with further excavations by Michele Gervasio in 1910, the corridor-type tomb is nearly 10 metres long with a burial chamber 1.80 m high [1] [2] [3]. Excavations uncovered pottery, stone knives, obsidian blades, and a bronze falera [2] [4]. In 2011 UNESCO recognized it as a Heritage Witness to a Culture of Peace [4] [5].

row.name: Skelhøj
row.description: Skelhøj is a burial mound from the early Bronze Age [1]. It was archaeologically excavated between 2002 and 2004 [1]. Skelhøj is an individual burial mound that is part of a broader series of 26 along the Kongeå River in Southern Denmark [1]. The mound was dated to the 15th century BC using radiocarbon dating [1]. The mound was divided into eight sections, evocative of an eight-spoked wheel, each of which were constructed independently, and the groups involved in construction may have brought turf from the area they lived in [1]. The mound was robbed, likely shortly after construction, and another time in the 19th century [1]. Archeologists sought to study how the burial mound's oak coffin was preserved along with what was within it, how the barrow was constructed, and what the landscape around the mound looked like when the mound was constructed [1]. They concluded that the coffin had been covered in large amounts of water shortly after burial, which created what they described as an "iron capsule" around the coffin through a chemical reduction reaction [1].

row.name: Kirkdale Cave
row.description: Kirkdale Cave is a cave and fossil site located in Kirkdale near Kirkbymoorside in the Vale of Pickering, North Yorkshire, England [1]. William Buckland analyzed the cave and its contents in December 1821 and determined that the bones were the remains of animals brought in by hyenas who used it for a den, and not a result of the Biblical flood floating corpses in from distant lands, as he had first thought [1]. The fossil bones found in the cave included those of straight-tusked elephants, hippopotamuses, the narrow-nosed rhinoceros, cave hyena, cave lion, Irish elk, brown bears, red deer and fallow deer [1]. The fossilized remains were embedded in a silty layer sandwiched between layers of stalagmite [1]. The entrance to the cave was found by limestone quarry workers in the summer of 1821 [1].

row.name: Tutuveni
row.description: Tutuveni is a prehistoric petroglyph site at the base of Echo Cliffs in Coconino County, Arizona [1]. The Hopi refer to it as "Tutuveni" meaning "Newspaper Rock" [1]. The site was used by young Hopi men during their ceremonial pilgrimages to Ongtupqa (the Grand Canyon) to mark their passage into adulthood [1]. They would stop and camp at the site and would etch their clan symbols onto the rocks, showing their participation and passage in that pilgrimage [1]. The site contains more than 5,000 Hopi clan symbols, dating from perhaps as early as 1200 to the 1950s, inscribed on eight sandstone boulders [1]. The petroglyphs, each around 10x10cm, are of iconic symbols representing animals, plants, or cultural items [1].

row.name: Aballava
row.description: Aballava was a Roman fortress on Hadrian's Wall situated about one and a half miles south of the Solway Firth, guarding the Peat Wath and Sandwath fords [1]. The fort stood between Petriana to the east and Coggabata to the west [1]. In the 3rd century AD, it housed a contingent of North African troops called the Aurelian Moors [1] [2]. A Roman altar found in 1934 near Beaumont records a dedication dated to AD 253-258 [3]. The fort appears in the Notitia Dignitatum as Aballaba and in the Ravenna Cosmography as Avalana [4] [5].

row.name: Aubrey Holes - Stonehenge
row.description: The Aubrey holes are a ring of 56 chalk pits at Stonehenge, named after seventeenth-century antiquarian John Aubrey [1]. They date to the earliest phases of Stonehenge in the late fourth and early third millennium BC [1]. 25 of the holes were excavated by Hawley in 1920 and seven more in 1924 [1]. In 1950 Stuart Piggott and Richard Atkinson dug two more Aubrey Holes which brought the total excavated to 35, including one that Richard Colt Hoare may have encountered whilst digging beneath the fallen Slaughter Stone in the early nineteenth century [1]. It was found that the pits were an average of 0.76m deep and 1.06m in diameter [1]. 25 of the pits contained later cremation burials inserted into their upper fills along with long bone pins which may have secured leather or cloth bags used to hold the remains [1]. Their presence makes Stonehenge Britain's oldest cremation cemetery [1].

row.name: Lismore Fields
row.description: Lismore Fields is a prehistoric settlement near the River Wye in Buxton, Derbyshire, discovered in 1984 by the Trent and Peak Archaeological Trust while searching for a Roman road [1]. Excavations revealed two Early Neolithic longhouses, among the best-preserved examples in Britain [2]. Building 1 dates to 3800-3650 BC and Building 2 to 3650-3350 BC [2]. The site yielded one of the largest cereal assemblages from any Early Neolithic site in England, possibly representing the earliest evidence of cereal cultivation in the British Isles [2]. It is a protected Scheduled Monument [1] [2].

row.name: Hypogeum of Torre del Ram
row.description: The Hypogeum of Torre del Ram is an archaeological site in Cala en Blanes, Ciutadella de Menorca [1]. It is a Bronze Age funerary hypogeum, used as a collective tomb by a family or a small community [1]. Even though it was emptied in later centuries and reused as a cattle shelter, causing the loss of all information regarding the interred population, grave goods, and chronology, its resemblance to other prehistoric tombs of Menorca dates it to between 1700 and 1400 BC [1]. A stepped corridor leads to the tomb's rectangular chamber, which has a stone bench that surrounds its internal perimeter [1]. Part of the stone gallery, which used to cover the corridor and the entrance, is still preserved; this was built using the Cyclopean technique [1]. The corridor is 2.60 m long, while the dimensions of the chamber are: 8.80 m long, 2.50 m wide, and 1.95 m high [1]. The walls of the internal chamber present several engravings representing three sailing ships and other undetermined figures [1].

row.name: El Pedregal Archaeological Site
row.description: El Pedregal is a rock art site in northwest Costa Rica, 20 km from the Nicaraguan border in the Cordillera de Guanacaste mountains [1] [2]. The site was first scientifically documented in 1989 and is catalogued in the Costa Rican National Museum's archaeological database under key G-540-Pd [1]. It forms part of the Guanacaste Conservation Area, which was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999 [3] [4].

row.name: Castle Folds
row.description: Castle Folds or Castlesteads was a Romano-British walled settlement on Great Asby Scar – an area of limestone pavement in the parish of Asby, Cumbria [1]. In medieval times, it was used as a shieling – a temporary summer shelter [1]. It is now in ruins but is protected as a scheduled monument [1]. The settlement covered most of a small knoll on the limestone pavement of the scar [1]. A walled enclosure surrounded most of the knoll and, on the western side, the eight-foot thick walls extended the steep escarpment of the knoll to form a significant obstacle [1]. The area enclosed is about 1.25 acres [1]. There were about a dozen stone huts built into the walls of the enclosure so that the central space was open [1]. The wall was constructed from orthostats which enclosed rubble [1].

row.name: Acidava
row.description: Acidava was a Dacian and later Roman town and fort on the Olt river near the lower Danube [1]. The settlement's remains are located in today's Enoşeşti, Olt County, Oltenia [1]. After the Roman conquest of Dacia by Roman Emperor Trajan, Acidava became a civilian and military centre, with castra being built in the area [1]. Acidava was part of the Limes Alutanus, a line of fortifications built under emperor Hadrian running north–south along the Alutus river [1]. The function of the limes was to monitor the Roxolani to the east and deter any possible attacks [1]. Acidava is depicted in the Tabula Peutingeriana between Romula and Rusidava [1].

row.name: Armeni - Archaeological Site
row.description: A remarkably preserved Late Minoan cemetery near Rethymno, Crete, containing 232 tombs dating to c. 1420-1190 BC [1] [2]. Finds include painted larnakes decorated with octopuses and hunting scenes, bronze weapons, sealstones, a boar's tusk helmet, and a stirrup jar inscribed in Linear B. All tomb entrances face east [1] [2].

row.name: Midsummer Hill
row.description: Midsummer Hill is an Iron Age hill fort situated in the Malvern Hills, a range extending approximately 13 km north-south along the Herefordshire-Worcestershire border [1] [2]. The fort spans Midsummer Hill and Hollybush Hill, lying to the south of Herefordshire Beacon with views toward Eastnor Castle [1]. At 284 metres elevation, the site occupies a position with Swinyard Hill to the north [1]. The hillfort is protected as a Scheduled Ancient Monument [1].

row.name: Menhirs of Lavajo
row.description: A group of menhirs in the parish of Alcoutim e Pereiro, Algarve, Portugal, likely erected during the second half of the 4th millennium BC [1] [2]. The largest stands over 3 metres tall and is carved from greywacke, a dark grey stone with a brown patinated surface, making it the largest example of greywacke menhirs known in Portugal [1] [2] [3]. The menhirs have an ellipsoidal cross-section and are engraved with circles and dimples [2] [4].

row.name: Lees Hall Roman Camp
row.description: Lees Hall Roman Camp is an archaeological site, a Roman camp near Hadrian's Wall, in Northumberland, England [1]. It is near Haltwhistle and adjacent to the B6318 road [1]. The camp is one of over 40 temporary Roman camps recorded near Hadrian's Wall; they may have been marching camps, or were occupied by troops constructing the wall, or were used during military training [1]. This camp is unusual in having an outwork surrounding the main defences, suggesting that it was used for more than one campaign season [1]. The camp, a scheduled monument, is about 1 kilometre south of Hadrian's Wall, and is 680 metres south of the Vallum [1]. There are extensive views to the north and east; a small stream lies within the fort [1]. It survives as earthworks and ditches; the rampart has an average height of 0.3 metres with an external ditch up to 0.4 metres deep [1]. It is rectangular, measuring 203 metres west to east by 140 metres north to south, enclosing an area of 1.7 hectares [1].

row.name: Mersinaki
row.description: Mersinaki is an ancient place located near the shore, between Vouni and Soli, in Cyprus [1]. The Swedish Cyprus Expedition, led by Einar Gjerstad, excavated Mersinaki during the year 1930 and found an open-air sanctuary by a river delta [1]. The sanctuary might have been dedicated to Apollon since two inscriptions mention him, but another inscription mentions Athena as well [1].

row.name: Scutchamer Knob
row.description: Scutchamer Knob, also known as Cuckhamsley Hill and occasionally as Scotsman's Knob or Beacon Hill, is an early Iron Age round barrow on the Ridgeway National Trail at East Hendred Down in the English county of Oxfordshire (formerly in Berkshire) [1]. Originally called Cwichelmeshlaew or Cwichelm's Barrow, it is recorded as having been the place where King Edwin of Northumbria killed Cwichelm of Wessex in AD 636 and, in the Middle Ages, became the meeting point of the shire moot which was abolished in 1620 [1]. It was long thought to be the actual burial place of Cwichelm but the mound has been excavated several times without serious finds [1]. In 1006, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle states that the Danes marched to Cuckhamsley Hill as they believed that if they reached the Hill, they would never return to the sea [1].

row.name: Welsh Way
row.description: The Welsh Way was a British Iron Age trade route and track-way that originally carried trade between South Wales and the Oxford area of England across the Cotswold Hills [1]. There is evidence it was utilised and improved by the Roman army following the conquest of Britain as a link between Akeman Street and the Fosse Way [1]. It links the highest navigable point on the River Thames at Lechlade to the lowest crossing point of the River Severn at Gloucester [1]. Originally it had a braided nature with one route through Quenington and another through Fairford [1]. The Welsh Way exists today as a named lane which leaves the Gloucester-Cirencester road before Duntisbourne and passes through Barnsley and Ready Token to Fairford and Lechlade [1].

row.name: Jabal al-ʿHayn
row.description: Jabal al-ʿHayn is a prominent outcrop of red sandstone in Saudi Arabia, known for its pre-historic petroglyphs, tribal markings (wusūm) and inscriptions in early Semitic languages as well as Arabic [1]. Ancient petroglyphs carved on the rock faces of Jabal al-ʿHayn depict horned bison, standing figures and an exceptional wild cat with a curling tail [1]. Camels are shown in some petroglyphs that seem to be less ancient [1]. Among the many inscriptions at Jabal al-ʿHayn are a number in Arabic which date to the earliest years of the Islamic calendar [1]. One inscription quotes Quran, Surah 18 Al-Kahf verse 21 [1]. The inscription was studied by Fred Donner and published in 1984 [1]. In a second record of singular historical importance, an individual named Rāfiʿ bin 'Alī declares "I believe that there is no God except Him in whom the children of Israel believed, (believing as) a Muslim Hanif; nor am I among the polytheists." This gives a direct quote of Quran, Surah 10 Yunus verse 90 [1]. Also published by Donner is an inscription on a boulder invoking the name of God and giving an exceptional religious maxim [1].

row.name: Iskanwaya
row.description: Iskanwaya is a pre-Columbian sacred site, situated on a mountain ridge above the Llica River in Bolivia, 325 km north of La Paz [1]. The sacred site of Iskanwaya is found on the edge of the Cordillera Real [1]. The site is located near Aucapata, a small town in the Muñecas Province, on the northern side of the Andean cordilleras [1]. The city of Iskanwaya was built on two platforms on an area of 0.6 square kilometers and was notable for its running water provided by a network of irrigation canals [1]. The irrigation system brought water from the Naranjani stream through canals and was distributed to the agglutinated Iskanwaya dwelling groups [1]. More than one hundred large buildings composed of stone masonry and an average of thirteen rooms have survived [1]. The Iskanwaya ruins go back to the Mollo culture which predated the Inca civilization and whose people presumably built the constructions as early as 800 BC or in their prime cultural period from 1145 to 1425 [1].

row.name: Zapote Bobal
row.description: Zapote Bobal is the modern name for a pre-Columbian Maya archaeological site located south of the San Pedro Martir river in the Petén department of Guatemala [1]. The name Zapote Bobal was coined by archaeologist Ian Graham, who discovered the site in the 1970s [1]. Built atop a leveled natural hill 1 kilometer long and 700 meters wide, the center of the site is characterized by a royal palace, several temple-pyramids, and elite residences [1]. Immediately outside this center are several mound groups, including one characterized by a pyramid 35 meters in height [1]. Although the general scale of construction at Zapote Bobal is quite large and would normally be characteristic of a long-lived ancient Maya center, it is clear that the city center was occupied for a brief period of time [1]. The royal dynasty at Zapote Bobal seems to have flourished for only 200 years, disintegrating by A.D. 800 [1]. For the majority of the Late Classic (AD 600-900), Zapote Bobal was the center of a kingdom that included the sites of Pajaral and (probably) La Joyanca [1].

row.name: Barton Creek Cave
row.description: Barton Creek Cave is a natural cave in Belize [1]. It is located in the upper Barton Creek area near San Ignacio in the Cayo District [1]. Barton Creek Cave is a primarily single-passage resurging stream cave [1]. By 2002 a cave survey had been completed by the Western Belize Regional Cave Project, recording a total of 6,400 m (21,000 ft) of passages; dye traces at sinking streams above the cave indicated that there could be a further 6 km (3.7 mi) of cave passages beyond the terminal sumps [1]. By 2005 the Xibalba Mapping and Exploration Team had extended the survey to 8 km (5.0 mi) [1]. In the early 1970s, several Mennonites from the nearby Mennonite community floated a short distance into Barton Creek Cave on oil drums [1]. They found human bones not far from the cave entrance [1].

row.name: Desilo
row.description: Desilo is an underwater archaeological site in southern Bosnia and Herzegovina, located near the Neretva river and the Croatian border [1]. Investigations led by Professor Snjezana Vasilj of the University of Mostar and her archaeological team, uncovered in 2007 many sunken boats at the bottom of the small lake in Desilo valley [1]. The archaeologists believe these boats to be Illyrian ships, dating back to the first and second centuries B.C. Further excavations in 2008 by University of Oslo archaeologists found evidence suggesting that Desilo was an Illyrian trading post [1]. The underwater archaeological site of Desilo was first discovered and recorded officially in 1972 [1]. The ships were covered with fragments of amphorae, Roman pitchers for holding wine [1]. Lindhagen and Prusac discovered the remains of a harbour buried in the river bed [1]. A polygonal wall 20 metres in length and 60 centimetres in width appeared solidly built [1]. Prusac and Lindhagen found an Illyrian settlement about a hundred metres from the harbour site [1].

row.name: Neolithic Dwellings Museum
row.description: Neolithic Dwellings Museum in Stara Zagora, Bulgaria is a museum in Stara Zagora, Bulgaria, which contains ruins of two of the oldest surviving buildings in the world [1]. The Neolithic Dwellings Museum is built around two Neolithic houses dating back to the 6th millennium BC [1]. 1826 artifacts were found there [1]. The Neolithic dwellings are the best-preserved in Europe from this period [1]. Kitchens, fireplaces, hand grain mills, and ceramic vessels comprise the richest inventory of 6th millennium BC prehistoric house life in Europe [1].

row.name: Sítio Arqueológico da Pedra Pintada
row.description: The Pedra Pintada or "Painted Rock" is a large rock formation in the state of Roraima [1]. It is 85 metres long, 35 metres high and 30 metres wide, with a cave underneath [1]. It is located on the Boa Vista savanna [1]. Rock art has been found on the walls of the cave as well as on the exterior of the rock, and the cave has yielded potsherds, axes, and beads [1]. During a study and excavations between 1985 and 1987, Brazilian archaeologists came to the conclusion that the site was inhabited as far back as 2000 BC [1]. They classified the rock art into two different styles: the abstract "Parime" and the realist "Surumu" [1]. The "Surumu" style is similar to the "Aishalton" style of the Caribbean Islands and the north of South America [1].

row.name: Main Limes
row.description: The Main Limes, also called the Nasser Limes, was built around 90 AD and, as part of the Upper Germanic-Rhaetian Limes, formed the frontier of the Roman Empire in the area between the present day villages of Großkrotzenburg and Bürgstadt [1]. In this section the limes adjoined the River Main (Moenus), which forms a natural boundary for about 50 kilometres here, so "Main" refers to the river [1]. However, of the many watchtowers that probably stood along the Main, to date only one south of Obernburg am Main has been identified [1]. North of the Main the limes initially runs through the marshy terrain of the Schifflache and Bulau before linking up with the Wetterau Limes [1]. At the crossing of the Main at Großkrotzenburg a Roman bridge has been identified from post sockets [1]. In the south it extended in its early period to Obernburg or Wörth [1].

row.name: Gazma Cave
row.description: Gazma Cave is a Paleolithic dwelling site discovered between Ordubad and Sharur districts in 1983 [1]. Gazma Cave is located 3 km northeast of Tananam village, 1450 m above the sea level [1]. Archeological excavations were carried out there under the leadership of A.G.Jafarov in 1987–1990, and A.Zeynalov in 2008–2013 [1]. In addition to fauna fossils, 874 stone tools were also discovered in the cave [1]. The form of the tools is similar to those derived from Azokh and Tağlar caves [1]. 6 cultural layers were discovered in the cave [1].

row.name: Caer Bran
row.description: Caer Bran Hill Fort is an archaeological site near Sancreed and Carn Euny Iron Age village, on the Penwith peninsula in Cornwall [1]. The site consists of an Iron Age hill fort which originally included a circular stone-lined inner wall, twelve feet thick, enclosing a space 200 feet in diameter [1]. Surrounding this was a ditch forty-five feet wide and seven feet deep, an earthen rampart fifteen feet high with stone revetment and a slight counterscarp outer bank [1]. There are remnants of a stone-lined causeway over the ditch at the original entrance to the North West adjacent to the ancient trackway linking Penzance with Land's End [1]. In the centre are the remains of a large circular stone building, of about fifty feet in diameter [1]. There are three Bronze Age ring cairns within the outer ramparts according to a Cornwall Archaeological Unit Survey [1].

row.name: Berry Camp
row.description: Berry Camp is a rectangular promontory hillfort located on a plateau, close to the cliff edge at Langham Field on Littlecombe Hill at Berry Cliff, Branscombe, Devon [1]. It is part of the Jurassic Coast World Heritage Site, which is also a Site of Special Scientific Interest [1]. The hillfort dates to the Iron Age and has an adjoining prehistoric field system [1]. Three sides of the defensive bank and ditch are visible today but the ditches have been used as a dumping ground and are partly filled in [1]. It is thought that a fourth side of the fort has been lost to coastal erosion [1].

row.name: Batham Gate
row.description: Batham Gate is the medieval name for a Roman road in Derbyshire which ran south-west from Templebrough on the River Don in South Yorkshire to Brough-on-Noe and the spa town of Buxton in Derbyshire [1]. Gate means "road" in northern English dialects; the name therefore means "road to the bath town" [1]. Batham Gate Road was assigned the Margary number RR710a [1]. A section of Batham Gate Road east of Peak Forest is a protected Scheduled Monument [1]. There are also modern roads called Batham Gate Road at Peak Dale, near Buxton, and at Bradwell, near Brough, which are remnants of the route of the original Roman road [1]. A Roman milestone was discovered in 1862 in the Silverlands district of Buxton [1]. It is the oldest inscribed milestone found in Derbyshire [1].

row.name: El Castillo de Huarmey
row.description: El Castillo de Huarmey is a pyramid-like structure on the coast of Peru, in the Ancash Region north of Lima [1]. The 2013 discovery at El Castillo de Huarmey of a royal Wari tomb containing 60 individuals and three burials of elite women suggests the need to reassess the Wari presence on the coast of Peru [1]. El Castillo de Huarmey was excavated in secret over the course of several months in 2013 to prevent looting [1]. The burial chamber of the royal tomb was discovered in early 2013 by a Peruvian-Polish research team [1]. The tomb contained 1,200 artifacts, including gold earrings, bronze axes, jewelry made of copper and silver, and silver bowls [1]. The tomb contained 60 human bodies buried in rows in a seated position and clothed in deteriorating textiles [1]. Three side chambers contained three bodies of royal Wari women whose bodies were accompanied by prized possessions, including gold weaving tools [1].

row.name: Innisidgen
row.description: Innisidgen is the site of two Bronze Age entrance graves on the island of St Mary's in the Isles of Scilly [1]. The two burial monuments, (Upper and Lower Innisidgen) lie on a steep slope of Innisidgen Hill overlooking Crow Sound with a view towards the Eastern Isles [1]. Innisidgen Hill is a scheduled monument on the Isles of Scilly, north east of Hugh Town [1]. Lower Innisidgen lies near the bottom of the northern slope of Innisidgen Hill [1]. This grave is more damaged than the upper grave and has only two of its original capstones [1]. Upper Innisidgen, also known as "The Giant's Grave", is one of the best preserved entrance graves on Scilly [1]. The entrance grave consists of a slightly oblong mound of earth and rubble measuring 9m by 8m, and is 1.8m in height [1]. The mound covers an intact burial chamber with an entrance at the eastern side of the mound [1].

row.name: Chaa Creek
row.description: Chaa Creek is a tributary of the Macal River in the Cayo District in western Belize [1]. It is near the site of an ancient Maya settlement [1]. Initial investigation and surveying of the site was done from 1992 to 1994 under the auspices of the Xunantunich Archaelogical Project [1]. Excavations were conducted in 1995 and 1997 [1]. Significant pottery finds and other artifacts have been recovered at the site, which is posited to be a satellite site of Xunantunich [1].

row.name: Kong Asgers Høj
row.description: Kong Asgers Høj is a large passage grave on the island of Møn in Denmark [1]. The megalithic structure dated to Neolithic Funnel Beaker culture [1]. The grave consists of a chamber (10 m long by 2 m wide) with a long passage (7.5 m long) [1]. Study of King Asger Høj began in 1839, when the Danish merchant Gustav Hage tried to find a treasure but found it empty [1]. The grave is structurally untouched since ancient times, but may have been cleared then [1].

row.name: Bülövqaya
row.description: Bülövqaya is a Chalcolithic archaeological settlement near the village of Göynük in the Babek District of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic, Azerbaijan [1]. The site lies on the left bank of the Sarısu River at an elevation of about 1,430 to 1,452 m and covers approximately 1.14 ha [1]. Radiocarbon dates place the principal occupation of the site in the early to mid-fifth millennium BC [1]. Excavated material includes plain and painted pottery, obsidian and flint tools, bone artefacts, architectural remains, hearths, storage pits and pottery kilns [1]. Excavation identified two construction levels distinguished by soil colour and structure [1]. An analysis of 74 obsidian specimens found that material from the Zangezur Mountains predominated, with a smaller component attributed to Meydan Dağ in eastern Anatolia [1]. The architectural remains indicate groups of light rectangular structures arranged around working areas [1].

row.name: Banwolseong
row.description: Wolseong or Wolseong Palace was a royal palace of Silla [1]. It was located in what is now Gyeongju [1]. The palace was used during the Silla and Unified Silla periods [1]. The palace gets its names from the approximate outline of the palace walls, which were shaped like a crescent moon [1]. It is also called Banwolseong or Sinwolseong or Jaeseong, which means where the king resides [1]. The South Korean government has also designated the palace ruins as Historic Site No. 16 [1].

row.name: Beech Bottom Dyke
row.description: Beech Bottom Dyke, is a large ditch running for almost a mile at the northern edge of St Albans, Hertfordshire, flanked by banks on both sides [1]. It is up to 30 m wide, and 10 m deep [1]. The dyke was constructed towards the end of the Iron Age, probably between 5 and 40 AD [1]. This, and other similar earthworks in the district, may have been built by the powerful Celtic tribe established in this area, the Catuvellauni, probably by King Cunobelinus to define areas of land around their tribal centre at Verlamion, the predecessor of the Roman city of Verulamium [1]. Beech Bottom Dyke is thought to have originally been part of a defensive system for a Belgic settlement [1].

row.name: Stoa Basileios
row.description: Stoa Basileios, meaning Royal Stoa, was a Doric stoa in the northwestern corner of the Athenian Agora, which was built in the 6th century BC, substantially altered in the 5th century BC, and then carefully preserved until the mid-second century AD [1]. It is among the smallest known Greek stoas, but had great symbolic significance as the seat of the Athenian King Archon, repository of Athens' laws, and site of "the stone" on which incoming magistrates swore their oath of office [1]. The Stoa was built in the Doric order, with solid walls on the north, west, and east sides and a colonnade of eight columns along the eastern side, facing towards the open space of the Agora [1]. It measures 17.72 metres long from north to south and 7.18 metres wide from east to west [1]. Ceramic finds in the foundation indicate a date after 575-550 BC [1]. In the 440s BC, the stoa was renovated [1]. In the 5th century BC, the Areopagos council sometimes met in the Stoa as well and a rope would be set up to keep people from interrupting its proceedings [1].

row.name: Kastelli Giant's Church
row.description: Kastelli Giant's Church is a prehistoric stone enclosure situated near Pattijoki in the North Ostrobothnia region of Finland [1]. It is one of the largest of forty such "Giant's Churches" to be found in this region of Finland [1]. It dates to around 2000 BC [1]. The Giant's Church at Kastelli is a rectangular stone enclosure measuring around 60 by 35 metres [1]. The walls are seven metres wide and survive to a height of two metres [1]. When built it would have been on a rocky shoreline [1]. The enclosure is surrounded by more than twenty stone cairns [1]. The site was excavated in the 1920s; it has been dated to around 2000 BC [1].

row.name: Shap Stone Avenue
row.description: Shap Stone Avenue sits near the centre of the Eden Valley, Cumbria [1]. It is broadly grouped into a category of monuments dubbed by Aubrey Burl, as 'Cumbrian Circles': large, uncluttered enclosures of stone [1]. The monuments around Shap form a northwest alignment with several monuments in the Eden Valley [1]. A significant burial cairn, known as 'Skellaw Hill', is found at the avenue's northern end, though most stones have now been lost [1]. The Goggleby Stone is about ten feet high and has a cup mark on its north face [1]. Tom Clare suggests that the avenues date to the Late Neolithic period (approximately 3,200 - 2,500 BC), based upon evidence supplied by the Goggleby Stone [1].

row.name: Romano-Gallic Baths of Entrammes
row.description: The Roman-Gaul Baths of Entrammes is a complex of Gallo-Roman thermal baths in Entrammes, Mayenne [1]. The baths were partially incorporated into a church with the hypocaust surviving below the new structure [1]. The remains were discovered in 1987 [1]. Archaeological surveys were done to reassess the church of Saint-Étienne [1]. A hypocaust in good condition was found below the church, confirming the presence of a thermal site of the 2nd century [1].

row.name: Għar Għerduf Catacombs
row.description: The Għar Għerduf catacombs at Ta' Kerċem, also known as Għar Gerduf, are the only surviving early Christian catacombs or paleochristian hypogea in Gozo [1]. Għar Għerduf is a unique Roman burial site in Gozo [1]. The catacombs are dug into the Globigerina Limestone, on the western slope of Lunzjata Valley [1]. Originally, the complex had a long corridor which extended for around 14 metres in an east–west direction [1]. A number of arcosolia are hewn into the walls [1]. Għar Gerduf suffered substantial mutilation during the second half of the nineteenth century [1]. Almost all the internal wall partitions aligning the arcosolia were chiselled down, while the floor was lowered by several metres to form two interlinking and split-level halls [1].

row.name: Roman Aqueduct of Vieu
row.description: The Roman aqueduct of Vieu is a Roman underground aqueduct, which is located in Vieu in the French department of Ain in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region [1]. The aqueduct has been the subject of historical studies since the seventeenth century [1]. According to R. Chevallier, a member of Robert Bedon's team, the dating of the aqueduct is uncertain, but estimated to be as old as about 150 AD [1].

row.name: Little Woodbury
row.description: Little Woodbury is the name of an Iron Age archaeological site in Britford parish, near Salisbury in the English county of Wiltshire [1]. The site lies about 1+1⁄4 miles south of the centre of Salisbury and 1 mile north of Odstock village [1]. It was partially excavated in 1938 and 1939 by Gerhard Bersu [1]. A settlement had been identified at the site through aerial archaeology by O.G.S. Crawford almost twenty years previously [1]. Bersu worked at the site from 12 June to 18 September 1938, and 12 June to 19 July 1939 [1]. He dug a network of 4-5m wide parallel trenches across the site [1]. By this method he was able to identify a large roundhouse and several other domestic features such as corn-drying frames, granaries, and storage pits [1]. The postholes of the roundhouse enabled Bersu to argue that these structures were the common domestic building type of the Iron Age; prior to his work it was thought that people lived in clusters of pit-dwellings in the ground [1].

row.name: Caerau Hillfort
row.description: Caerau Hillfort is a large triangular multivallate Iron Age hillfort, built on a previously occupied Neolithic site, occupying the western tip of an extensive ridge-top plateau in the western suburbs of Caerau and Ely, Cardiff, Wales [1]. Excavations for an episode of Channel 4's Time Team showed the hillfort's occupation began about 600 BC [1]. Further excavations, in 2013–2014, revealed evidence of the site's occupation back to the early Neolithic [1]. Finds included flint tools and weapons dating to 3600 BC [1].

row.name: Willy Howe
row.description: Willy Howe (also Willey-Hou) is a tumulus in the Yorkshire Wolds, East Riding of Yorkshire [1]. Willy Howe is a large round barrow 7.5 m (25 ft) high, located between Wold Newton and Burton Fleming in the civil parish of Thwing [1]. The mound has been recorded as being excavated several times: by Lord Londesborough in 1857; and by Canon William Greenwell in 1887 [1]. Neither found burials or grave goods; Greenwell found a feature approximating a shallow grave [1].
