row.old_value: A settlement with ceramics resembling Dalma-type pottery from northwestern Iran. The painted wares link this site to a broad cultural network spanning the 5th millennium BC.
row.new_value: Radiocarbon dates place the principal occupation of the site in the early to mid-fifth millennium BC.

row.old_value: Built 1438–1530 AD. Perched at 3,750 metres on the Inca Trail, its semicircular rooms served as a royal rest stop and surveillance post. In Quechua its name means 'basket-shaped.'
row.new_value: The ruins lie on the southern slope of the mountain Runkuraqay near the Runkuraqay pass.

row.old_value: At 7 metres tall and roughly 18 tonnes, the largest fully human-carved menhir on the peninsula. Found fallen near Castelo de Vide, it was later re-erected on its hilltop in the Serra de São Mamede.
row.new_value: The monolith, consisting of coarse-grained porphyroid granite, was discovered in a rural area, now used mainly for cork production, in 1965.

row.old_value: A Neolithic henge with 13 small standing stones forming an oval horseshoe that echoes the earliest form of Stonehenge. Its name translates as "Arthur's Grave."
row.new_value: Bedd Arthur consists of a barely visible oval bank and ditch, with thirteen standing stones, none higher than 60 centimetres arranged inside along with two further fallen stones.

row.old_value: A 6-metre-high boulder split perfectly in two, both halves balanced on small pedestals. Its southeast face is covered in ancient petroglyphs. No one agrees on what split it.
row.new_value: The rock is about 6 metres high and 9 metres wide, and is covered on its south-east face with numerous petroglyphs, including depictions of horses and ibex.

row.old_value: A granite boulder carved with flowing La Tene spirals from 300 BC-100 AD. Only three other decorated stones of this type exist in the entire country.
row.new_value: The Castlestrange stone is located in the grounds of Castlestrange House near Athleague in County Roscommon.

row.old_value: Uncovered during railway construction near modern Thessaloniki, this 4th-century BC farmhouse yielded olive remains that gave researchers a detailed picture of ancient oil production.
Timber post-holes at this Buxton site date to around 5000 BC, preserving rectangular Neolithic buildings. Charred grain here is among the earliest direct evidence of farming in the north.
2nd-century AD Roman camp near Hadrian's Wall with an outwork surrounding its main defences, suggesting specialised use beyond a standard marching camp. One of over 40 camps recorded near the Wall.
9th–4th century BC. Excavated in 1930 by the Swedish Cyprus Expedition, Mersinaki's river-delta sanctuary yielded large terracotta sculptures of bearded males, now in Stockholm's Medelhavsmuseet.
row.new_value: The sanctuary might have been dedicated to Apollon since two inscriptions mention him, but another inscription mentions Athena as well.

row.old_value: Petroglyphs of horned bison, standing figures, and a wild cat with a curling tail carved into red sandstone. Some carvings date to 7000 BC.
A pre-Columbian city on a mountain ridge with over 100 large buildings and running water. In extent and age it surpasses Machu Picchu.
row.new_value: The city of Iskanwaya was built on two platforms on an area of 0.6 square kilometers and was notable for its running water provided by a network of irrigation canals.

row.old_value: Built atop a leveled natural hill 1 km long in the Petén, this 600–800 AD Maya center pairs a royal palace and temple-pyramids with an unusually high density of royal stelae for its size.
row.new_value: The royal dynasty at Zapote Bobal seems to have flourished for only 200 years, disintegrating by A.D. 800.

row.old_value: Built around 90 AD. The Main Limes used the River Main as a 50 km natural barrier reinforced by watchtowers. Part of the Upper Germanic-Rhaetian Limes — now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A Paleolithic cave dwelling with over 17,000 animal bone fossils documenting the region's Ice Age fauna. Stone tools found here span tens of thousands of years.
row.new_value: Gazma Cave is a Paleolithic dwelling site discovered between Ordubad and Sharur districts in 1983.

row.old_value: The largest passage grave on its island, with a 10-metre chamber and a 7.5-metre passage. Investigation began in 1839 when a merchant went treasure hunting.
row.new_value: The grave is structurally untouched since ancient times, but may have been cleared then.

row.old_value: Rectangular — 60 by 35 metres — with 7-metre-wide walls and six gateways, this 2000 BC stone enclosure near Pattijoki is the largest of forty such 'Giant's Churches' in this region.
row.new_value: The Giant's Church at Kastelli is a rectangular stone enclosure measuring around 60 by 35 metres.

row.old_value: A 3.2 km megalithic avenue of stones linking stone circles and burial mounds, built 3000–2000 BC. One of only three such complexes in the region.
row.new_value: A significant burial cairn, known as 'Skellaw Hill', is found at the avenue's northern end, though most stones have now been lost.

row.old_value: Home to the earliest known Trincheras village, with 160 stone structure foundations from the ancient Hohokam people. The site dates back to at least 2100 BC.
row.new_value: Tumamoc Hill is a butte located immediately west of "A" Mountain and downtown Tucson.

row.old_value: Vast ruin complex in two river valleys occupied from 3600 to 200 BC. Sechin Bajo contains a circular plaza from around 3500 BC -- among the earliest monumental spaces yet found in the Americas.
row.new_value: The area of the Casma/Sechin culture extended about 40 kilometres inland from the sea. Radiocarbon dating indicates a plaza at Sechin Bajo was constructed in 3500 BCE.

row.old_value: Doric stoa from around 500 BC, seat of the Archon Basileus and repository of Athenian law. Incoming magistrates swore their oaths on a sacred stone kept within its walls.
row.new_value: In the 5th century BC, the Areopagos council sometimes met in the Stoa as well and a rope would be set up to keep people from interrupting its proceedings.

row.old_value: A Neolithic henge 85 metres across, later converted into a Roman amphitheatre and then refortified as an artillery position in the Civil War of the 1640s. Three civilizations reshaped the same ring.
row.new_value: Maumbury Rings was remodelled in the Roman period when it was adapted for use as an amphitheatre for the use of the citizens of the nearby Roman town of Durnovaria.

row.old_value: 1000–1500 AD. A pre-Inca site at 4,000 m atop Mullu Q'awa mountain in Espinar Province — near the village of Molloccahua, in a high-altitude landscape that tested everyone who chose to settle here.
row.new_value: The site was declared a National Cultural Heritage by Resolution No. 954-2010- INC on April 27, 2010.

row.old_value: Paleo-Christian catacombs that grew over 500 years into four underground complexes. Small compared to Rome's, they still rank with the most significant early Christian sites south of Rome.
row.new_value: In the post-Roman period, the largest catacomb was enlarged and turned into a small church.

row.old_value: A chambered long barrow from around 5000 BC. Part of the Medway Megaliths group — a cluster of Neolithic tombs built in a style repeated across the region.
row.new_value: In the 12th or 13th century, the chamber was dug into and heavily damaged, either by treasure hunters or iconoclastic Christians.

row.old_value: Hyena den 121,000 years old — bones of elephants, rhinos, hippos and cave lions found here in 1821. The northernmost hippo remains ever found. Buckland's analysis earned the Copley Medal in 1822.
row.new_value: Kirkdale Cave is a cave and fossil site located in Kirkdale near Kirkbymoorside in the Vale of Pickering, North Yorkshire.

row.old_value: Houses two of the oldest surviving buildings in the world, dating to the 6th millennium BC. Over 1,800 artifacts were found inside these Neolithic dwellings.
row.new_value: The Neolithic Dwellings Museum is built around two Neolithic houses dating back to the 6th millennium BC.

row.old_value: Two Bronze Age entrance graves on a steep slope overlooking the sea, dating to 2500-1000 BC. The larger measures 8 metres in diameter with a long entrance passage.
row.new_value: Innisidgen is the site of two Bronze Age entrance graves on the island of St Mary's in the Isles of Scilly.

row.old_value: A Roman underground aqueduct from the 2nd century AD, classified as a historic monument since 1840. It has survived almost 2,000 years underground.
row.new_value: According to R. Chevallier, a member of Robert Bedon's team, the dating of the aqueduct is uncertain, but estimated to be as old as about 150 AD.

row.old_value: Triangular multivallate fort in the suburbs of Cardiff, built on a previously occupied Neolithic site. At over 13 hectares, it ranks as the largest hilltop fortress in the south of the country.
row.new_value: Excavations for an episode of Channel 4's Time Team showed the hillfort's occupation began about 600 BC.

row.old_value: Inhabited for nearly 2,000 years from 900 BC, this southern Maya lowland site sits atop a partly artificial limestone acropolis. Its Maya name means stone set in earth.
row.new_value: On a limestone acropolis, over 40 masonry structures of Pacbitun ring its plazas. The Maya lived here from circa 900 BCE and abandoned it by about 900 CE, for reasons that remain unclear.

row.old_value: The ruins lie on the southern slope of the mountain Runkuraqay near the Runkuraqay pass.
row.new_value: Southeast of Machu Picchu, the ruins of Runkuraqay cling to the southern slope of the mountain that shares their name, near its pass. Hiram Bingham III visited in April 1915.

row.old_value: Buddhist monastery near Ghazni displaying two successive artistic phases: Hellenistic sculpture from the 3rd–6th century AD, then Sinicized-Indian styles from the 7th–9th century.
row.new_value: Dominating the Dasht-i Manara plain near Ghazni, Tepe Sardar is the ruin of a Buddhist stupa and monastery, destroyed by a great fire in the 7th century, then rebuilt and expanded.

row.old_value: Hopi petroglyph site at Echo Cliffs, used from ~1200 AD into the 1950s. Over 5,000 clan symbols on eight boulders - a rite-of-passage registry for young men making pilgrimages to the Grand Canyon.
row.new_value: At the base of Echo Cliffs, young Hopi men on pilgrimage to the Grand Canyon etched their clan symbols into Tutuveni: more than 5,000 of them, on eight sandstone boulders.

row.old_value: A ring of 56 chalk pits from 3100 BC, the earliest phase of Stonehenge. They held cremated human remains — Stonehenge was a cemetery before it was a monument.
row.new_value: At Stonehenge, a ring of 56 chalk pits, the Aubrey Holes, dates to its earliest phases. 25 of them later held cremation burials, making Stonehenge Britain's oldest cremation cemetery.

row.old_value: The city of Iskanwaya was built on two platforms on an area of 0.6 square kilometers and was notable for its running water provided by a network of irrigation canals.
row.new_value: On a mountain ridge above the Llica River, the sacred site of Iskanwaya spreads over two platforms, where canals from the Naranjani stream once brought running water to its stone dwellings.

row.old_value: Royal palace of the Silla dynasty from 57 BC to 938 AD, its crescent-moon-shaped walls gave it the name Half Moon Fortress. The palace grounds are today a public park in Gyeongju.
row.new_value: Walls shaped like a crescent moon gave Banwolseong its name: a royal palace of Silla in what is now Gyeongju, used through both the Silla and Unified Silla periods.

row.old_value: A 7.5-meter-high tumulus in the Wolds that yielded no burial despite multiple excavations. Medieval folklore connected it to fairies and hidden treasure.
row.new_value: In the Yorkshire Wolds rises Willy Howe, a round barrow 7.5 m high. Dug in 1857 and 1887, it gave up no burials or grave goods, though Greenwell found a feature like a shallow grave.

row.old_value: A Neolithic burial chamber capped by a massive roof slab estimated at 25 tonnes. Inside, the remains of 15 to 30 people were found — a communal tomb used over generations.
row.new_value: Under a roof slab estimated at 25 tonnes, the uprights of Lligwy Burial Chamber on Anglesey hide half their height underground. In 1909 excavators found the remains of some 15 to 30 people.

row.old_value: Two granite boulders near Øster Velling carry engraved geometric patterns from the Bronze Age — ships, sun discs, and other symbols. The stones were moved 50 metres from their original find spot.
row.new_value: In Øster Velling Skov forest, two granite boulders at Mandbjerghøj bear Bronze Age concentric rings and ovals, the same motif found on a gilt belt-hook in the grave of the nearby tumulus.

row.old_value: The highest hill in its county at 540 metres, with several Iron Age hillforts. Quarrying destroyed two of the three forts, leaving only Nordy Bank intact.
row.new_value: On Brown Clee Hill, the highest hill in Shropshire, Nordy Bank's ramparts still rise up to three metres, the last survivor of three Iron Age hill forts; two were largely lost to quarrying.

row.old_value: A 3rd-century dam across the Carenque River near Sintra, built to supply Olisipo (Lisbon) with water. Its mortar-bonded masonry survives partially buried beneath a modern road.
row.new_value: Built in the 3rd century to serve Olisipo, the Roman Dam of Belas keeps a segment some 15.5 metres long, braced by three buttresses, its channel still crossing the Águas Livres Aqueduct.

row.old_value: Built around 3000 BC on Sanday in Orkney — modelled closely on Maeshowe — this Neolithic cairn contained skeletal remains of multiple individuals when first opened in 1867.
row.new_value: On the Elsness peninsula of Sanday, Orkney, the Quoyness Chambered Cairn rests on an oval stone platform. Probably built around 3000 BC, it gave up the bones of several people in 1867.

row.old_value: A Bronze Age funerary hypogeum from 1700-1400 BC, emptied centuries ago and reused as cattle shelter. A rare vertical stone doorway still blocks the entrance.
row.new_value: A stepped corridor leads into the Hypogeum of Torre del Ram, a Bronze Age tomb whose chamber is ringed by a stone bench, its walls engraved with three sailing ships and undetermined figures.

row.old_value: A Dacian fortress that became a Roman military post on the Limes Alutanus under Emperor Hadrian. The fortified line ran north-south along the Olt River.
row.new_value: On the Olt river near the lower Danube, Acidava grew from a Dacian town into a Roman fort on the Limes Alutanus, a line of fortifications set to watch the Roxolani to the east.

row.old_value: A Maya cave where pottery and human remains were placed on ledges deep inside. The Maya treated caves as entrances to Xibalba, the underworld of the dead.
row.new_value: In the early 1970s Mennonites floated on oil drums into Barton Creek Cave and found human bones not far from its entrance. By 2005 the survey of its stream passages had reached 8 km.

row.old_value: The Neolithic Dwellings Museum is built around two Neolithic houses dating back to the 6th millennium BC.
row.new_value: In Stara Zagora, the Neolithic Dwellings Museum shelters two houses of the 6th millennium BC, the best-preserved of their period in Europe, with kitchens, fireplaces and hand grain mills.
Around 90 AD the Main Limes made the River Main itself a Roman frontier for about 50 kilometres. Of the many watchtowers that probably stood along it, only one has been identified to date.

row.old_value: Gazma Cave is a Paleolithic dwelling site discovered between Ordubad and Sharur districts in 1983.
row.new_value: Gazma Cave, a Paleolithic dwelling site 1450 m above sea level, revealed 6 cultural layers, fauna fossils and 874 stone tools, similar in form to those from Azokh and Tağlar caves.

row.old_value: Maya ruins largely unexcavated in the Macal River catchment, positioned as a satellite site of Xunantunich. What lies beneath this jungle floor remains mostly untouched.
row.new_value: Near Chaa Creek, a tributary of the Macal River in western Belize, lies an ancient Maya settlement, posited to be a satellite of Xunantunich, where significant pottery was recovered.

row.old_value: The grave is structurally untouched since ancient times, but may have been cleared then.
row.new_value: On the island of Møn, a 7.5 m passage leads into the 10 m chamber of Kong Asgers Høj, a Neolithic passage grave. In 1839 a merchant came seeking treasure and found it empty.

row.old_value: Gallo-Roman baths from the 2nd century AD, partially built into a church with the hypocaust heating system preserved beneath the nave.
row.new_value: Part of the Romano-Gallic Baths of Entrammes lives on inside a church in Mayenne, and beneath it lies a hypocaust in good condition, proof of 2nd century thermal baths discovered in 1987.

row.old_value: The only surviving Early-Christian catacombs in Gozo — a unique Roman burial site that has drawn scholarly attention for centuries.
row.new_value: Dug into Globigerina Limestone on a slope of Lunzjata Valley, the Għar Għerduf Catacombs are the only surviving early Christian catacombs in Gozo, with arcosolia hewn into their walls.

row.old_value: According to R. Chevallier, a member of Robert Bedon's team, the dating of the aqueduct is uncertain, but estimated to be as old as about 150 AD.
row.new_value: Running underground in the Ain, the Roman Aqueduct of Vieu has been studied since the seventeenth century. By R. Chevallier's account its date is uncertain, estimated as old as about 150 AD.

row.old_value: An Iron Age farmstead from around 800 BC that became a model for understanding how ordinary people lived in prehistoric Britain. Its grain storage pits reveal a sophisticated agricultural system.
row.new_value: In 1938 and 1939, trenches across Little Woodbury revealed a roundhouse, granaries and storage pits. From its postholes Gerhard Bersu argued roundhouses, not pits, were the Iron Age home.

row.old_value: The monolith, consisting of coarse-grained porphyroid granite, was discovered in a rural area, now used mainly for cork production, in 1965.
row.new_value: Found in two pieces in 1965 and rejoined in the 1990s, the Menhir of Meada measures about 7.5 metres, weighs around 18 tons and is believed to have been raised around 5000 BCE.

row.old_value: A site with Roman and Saxon pottery and an Anglo-Saxon cemetery. The hillside earthworks were noted as early as 1832 as possible ancient defenses.
row.new_value: Ploughing disturbed remains on Welbeck Hill; excavations began in 1962 at an Anglo-Saxon cemetery: burials along the hill crest, cremations on the eastern slope, 76 graves by July 1976.

row.old_value: A 32-km Roman road linking two forts and passing through some of the most remote terrain in the province. It connected the Hadrian's Wall garrison at Carvoran to supply bases further south.
row.new_value: For roughly 20 miles the Maiden Way ran from Bravoniacum to Magnis on Hadrian's Wall, a Roman shortcut supplying the Wall and lead and silver mines, later used as a drovers' road.

row.old_value: A 4.45-hectare prehistoric landscape with multiple monument types spanning millennia. Tombs, standing stones, and field boundaries all share the same patch of ground.
row.new_value: Cairns, standing stones, a barrow and three types of grave fill the Ballygroll Prehistoric Landscape, ranging from the Neolithic to the Late Bronze Age. Most have not been fully excavated.

row.old_value: Perched 4,126 metres up, Jach'a Phasa holds over 50 chullpa burial towers of volcanic stone and mud-and-straw mortar rising from a mountaintop enclosed by a perimeter wall.
row.new_value: At 4,126 metres, on a mountaintop north of the Mawri River, Jach'a Phasa is covered with more than 50 chullpa of volcanic stone and mortar of mud and straw, all surrounded by a wall.
Earthworks and ditches near Haltwhistle mark Lees Hall Roman Camp, about 1 kilometre south of Hadrian's Wall. An unusual outwork rings its defences, hinting at more than one campaign season.

row.old_value: The royal dynasty at Zapote Bobal seems to have flourished for only 200 years, disintegrating by A.D. 800.
row.new_value: On a leveled hill in the Petén, Zapote Bobal raised a royal palace and temple-pyramids, yet its royal dynasty seems to have flourished for only 200 years, disintegrating by A.D. 800.

row.old_value: A massive Iron Age ditch 30 metres wide and 10 metres deep running for nearly a mile. It may have served as a tribal boundary rather than a military fortification.
row.new_value: At the northern edge of St Albans, Beech Bottom Dyke runs almost a mile between banks on both sides, a ditch up to 30 m wide and 10 m deep, built probably between 5 and 40 AD.

row.old_value: The Giant's Church at Kastelli is a rectangular stone enclosure measuring around 60 by 35 metres.
row.new_value: When built, Kastelli Giant's Church would have stood on a rocky shoreline: a stone enclosure of around 60 by 35 metres, its walls seven metres wide, ringed by more than twenty cairns.

row.old_value: A two-story Early Bronze Age building from 2500 BC with baked clay roof tiles -- among the earliest tiled roofs in the world. The tiles gave it its modern name.
row.new_value: At Lerna, the House of the Tiles rose two stories under a roof of baked tiles; thousands of its terracotta tiles lay fallen in the debris. Fire finally destroyed it in the 22nd century BC.

row.old_value: Kirkdale Cave is a cave and fossil site located in Kirkdale near Kirkbymoorside in the Vale of Pickering, North Yorkshire.
row.new_value: Quarry workers found Kirkdale Cave in 1821. Inside lay bones of hippopotamuses, elephants and cave lions, brought not by the Biblical flood but by hyenas that used it as a den.

row.old_value: Known as Cwichelm's Barrow, this Iron Age round barrow on the Oxfordshire Ridgeway marks where King Edwin killed Cwichelm of Wessex in 636 AD. It later served as the shire moot meeting point.
row.new_value: In 1006, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says, Danes marched to Scutchamer Knob, an early Iron Age round barrow, believing that if they reached the hill they would never return to the sea.

row.old_value: Sunken boats at the bottom of a small lake, dating to the 1st–2nd century BC. Archaeologists identified them as Illyrian ships — a rare find of ancient watercraft.
row.new_value: In 2007, many sunken boats were uncovered in a small lake at Desilo, believed to be Illyrian ships of the first and second centuries B.C. and covered with fragments of amphorae.

row.old_value: A Roman road whose medieval name means "road to the bath town" -- it led to the spa at Buxton. Sections of the original route are now protected monuments.
row.new_value: Batham Gate means road to the bath town: a Roman road running from the River Don to the spa town of Buxton, where in 1862 the oldest inscribed milestone found in Derbyshire turned up.

row.old_value: Excavations for an episode of Channel 4's Time Team showed the hillfort's occupation began about 600 BC.
row.new_value: Caerau Hillfort crowns a ridge-top plateau in Cardiff, an Iron Age fort occupied from about 600 BC, yet built on a Neolithic site where flint tools and weapons dating to 3600 BC were found.

row.old_value: Maumbury Rings was remodelled in the Roman period when it was adapted for use as an amphitheatre for the use of the citizens of the nearby Roman town of Durnovaria.
row.new_value: Maumbury Rings, a Neolithic henge in Dorchester, hides a ditch of up to 45 shafts cut up to 11 metres deep into the chalk. In the Roman period it was remodelled as an amphitheatre.

row.old_value: The site was declared a National Cultural Heritage by Resolution No. 954-2010- INC on April 27, 2010.
row.new_value: On the summit of a mountain that shares its name, about 4,000 m up in the Cusco Region, lies Mullu Q'awa, an archaeological site declared a National Cultural Heritage in 2010.

row.old_value: The area of the Casma/Sechin culture extended about 40 kilometres inland from the sea. Radiocarbon dating indicates a plaza at Sechin Bajo was constructed in 3500 BCE.
row.new_value: Along the Casma and Sechin rivers, the ruins of the Casma-Sechin Culture reach toward the Pacific. By 3000 BC people here were building pyramids; a plaza at Sechin Bajo dates to 3500 BCE.

row.old_value: Mountain ruins at 4,150 metres elevation, one of countless unnamed Andean sites still waiting for systematic study. Its builders and purpose remain undocumented.
row.new_value: On top of a Peruvian mountain of the same name, the ruins of Huacramarca sit at 4,150 metres, their name possibly drawn from the Quechua words for horn and village.

row.old_value: A large boulder cairn surrounded by a stone ring and a human effigy figure, dating to about 1400 AD. The effigy is one of few such figures found on the northern plains.
row.new_value: On the Suffield Block in Alberta lies the British Block Cairn, dating from around 1400 CE: a large boulder cairn surrounded by a ring of stones and a human effigy figure.

row.old_value: Around 900 AD, the Chachapoyas placed mummies in cliff-side tombs above a high-altitude lake. Laguna de las Momias yielded extraordinary burials; condors overhead gave this Amazonian site its names.
row.new_value: At Laguna de las Momias, six mausoleums built against the rock held approximately two hundred funeral deposits, each a seated mummy in textiles, in caves painted with indecipherable symbols.

row.old_value: An Iron Age fortress whose walls have almost entirely collapsed. Large stone piles mark where fortifications and interior structures once stood.
row.new_value: On a hill outside the village of Ushi, the Iron Age fortress of Ushiberd has almost completely collapsed: stretches of wall line the hill's edge, and great piles of stone fill its interior.

row.old_value: The world's earliest known public museum, dating to 530 BC. Curated by Princess Ennigaldi, daughter of the last Babylonian king, near the Ziggurat of Ur.
row.new_value: Near the Ziggurat of Ur lay dozens of artifacts, centuries apart in age, set neatly side by side with clay labels: Ennigaldi-Nanna's Museum, the earliest known public museum, circa 530 BCE.
Work on the Athens to Thessaloniki railway uncovered an ancient farmhouse at Tria Platania, where a study of olive remains traced how oil was made from the fourth to the second century BC.

row.old_value: A Neolithic entrance grave considered one of the smallest and best-preserved in Britain. The circular mound is built of rubble and soil, typical of the Scillonian entrance type.
row.new_value: In a pasture by the upper Lamorna River, Brane Barrow, a Neolithic entrance grave ringed by granite blocks, shelters a stone-lined chamber roofed with two capstones. A third was removed.

row.old_value: In the 12th or 13th century, the chamber was dug into and heavily damaged, either by treasure hunters or iconoclastic Christians.
row.new_value: Near Addington in Kent, the sarsen chamber of Chestnuts Long Barrow held cremated and inhumed remains of at least nine or ten people, with arrow heads, pottery sherds and a clay pendant.

row.old_value: The sanctuary might have been dedicated to Apollon since two inscriptions mention him, but another inscription mentions Athena as well.
row.new_value: Between Vouni and Soli, by a river delta, the Swedish Cyprus Expedition uncovered the open-air sanctuary of Mersinaki in 1930. Two inscriptions name Apollon, but another names Athena.

row.old_value: Clifftop fort at 140 metres on the Devon coast, part of the Jurassic Coast World Heritage Site. Coastal erosion steadily consumes the ramparts -- the sea is slowly reclaiming the site.
row.new_value: On a plateau near the cliff edge at Branscombe, the Iron Age hillfort of Berry Camp still shows three sides of bank and ditch. The fourth is thought lost to coastal erosion.

row.old_value: Innisidgen is the site of two Bronze Age entrance graves on the island of St Mary's in the Isles of Scilly.
row.new_value: On a steep slope above Crow Sound, Innisidgen keeps two Bronze Age entrance graves. The upper, known as the Giant's Grave, holds an intact burial chamber under a mound of earth and rubble.

row.old_value: In the 5th century BC, the Areopagos council sometimes met in the Stoa as well and a rope would be set up to keep people from interrupting its proceedings.
row.new_value: In the northwestern corner of the Athenian Agora stood Stoa Basileios, among the smallest known Greek stoas, yet it kept Athens' laws and the stone on which new magistrates swore their oath.

row.old_value: A significant burial cairn, known as 'Skellaw Hill', is found at the avenue's northern end, though most stones have now been lost.
row.new_value: In the Eden Valley, Shap Stone Avenue ends at a burial cairn, Skellaw Hill. Its Goggleby Stone, cup-marked on its north face, led Tom Clare to suggest a Late Neolithic date.

row.old_value: Neolithic timber circle in Staffordshire dated 4100–2500 BC, with around 225 postholes invisible at ground level but visible as cropmarks from the air. Scheduled and still largely unexcavated.
row.new_value: Near the River Trent, the Catholme Ceremonial Complex is a Neolithic site that Birmingham Archaeology investigated from 2002 to 2004 with a geophysical survey, Lidar and excavation.

row.old_value: An Iron Age earthwork with two concentric banks and ditches encircling two leveled hut platforms. Small but strategic, it sits within what is now a national nature reserve.
row.new_value: Two concentric banks and ditches make Goosehill Camp, an Iron Age earthwork in the Kingley Vale National Nature Reserve on the South Downs, first excavated on record between 1953 and 1955.

row.old_value: Tumamoc Hill is a butte located immediately west of "A" Mountain and downtown Tucson.
row.new_value: West of downtown Tucson rises Tumamoc Hill, once home to the ancient Hohokam: 160 round stone foundations of the earliest known trincheras village, walls of stone and over 460 petroglyphs.

row.old_value: Bedd Arthur consists of a barely visible oval bank and ditch, with thirteen standing stones, none higher than 60 centimetres arranged inside along with two further fallen stones.
row.new_value: Inside a barely visible bank and ditch stand the unexcavated stones of Bedd Arthur, none over 60 centimetres, in a shape called a rectangle, a horseshoe, an oval and a pointed ellipse.

row.old_value: The rock is about 6 metres high and 9 metres wide, and is covered on its south-east face with numerous petroglyphs, including depictions of horses and ibex.
row.new_value: South of the Tayma oasis stands Al Naslaa, a sandstone rock split neatly in two, both halves balanced on small pedestals, its south-east face covered in petroglyphs of horses and ibex.

row.old_value: Classic Maya city active 550–950 AD, split into five numbered sub-sites along the Mopan River. A triadic complex in Plaza C signals participation in pan-Maya political and religious networks.
row.new_value: Sacul, a Maya city on a trade route through the Maya Mountains, lost a war to Ixkun in AD 779. Just 11 years later its king Ch'iyel visited Ixkun, and the two appear to have become allies.

row.old_value: A Minoan peak sanctuary from 2300-1700 BC where worshippers left clay figurines of humans and animals. Peak sanctuaries were mountaintop shrines visible for kilometres.
row.new_value: On the twin peaks of Atsipades in western Crete, Minoans held their religious rites. The autumn equinox can be seen between the peaks, and rock clefts hold votive figurines and bowls.

row.old_value: The Castlestrange stone is located in the grounds of Castlestrange House near Athleague in County Roscommon.
row.new_value: Flowing La Tène spirals decorate the Castlestrange Stone, an Iron Age granite boulder. Only three other stones of this type have been found in Ireland; all four lie on roughly the same line.

row.old_value: In the post-Roman period, the largest catacomb was enlarged and turned into a small church.
row.new_value: Dug from a quarry face in Rabat, the Abbatija Tad-Dejr Hypogeal Complex holds a stone altar and rock-carved crosses. Its largest catacomb became a small church; it also served as cow pens.

row.old_value: A 15th-century BC Bronze Age burial mound near the Kongeå River. It is part of a chain of 26 mounds along the river — a landscape of the dead.
row.new_value: Skelhøj, a Bronze Age mound of the 15th century BC, rose in sections like a spoked wheel; water covered its oak coffin soon after burial, forming what archaeologists call an iron capsule.

row.old_value: Walled settlement on Great Asby Scar limestone pavement in Cumbria, with walls 2.4 metres thick enclosing most of a small knoll. Later reused as a medieval summer shepherds shelter.
row.new_value: On the limestone pavement of Great Asby Scar lie the ruins of Castle Folds, a Romano-British walled settlement where about a dozen stone huts were built into the walls around an open centre.

row.old_value: An Iron Age trade route crossing the Cotswolds, linking the Thames to the Severn. The Romans later upgraded it to connect their major roads Akeman Street and the Fosse Way.
row.new_value: The Welsh Way, a British Iron Age trade route across the Cotswold Hills, links the highest navigable point on the Thames at Lechlade to the lowest crossing of the Severn at Gloucester.

row.old_value: Around 2000 BC, abstract images and what may be a calendar were carved into rock here — the most intriguing petroglyphs in the region. Whether it charts seasons or stars remains unanswered.
row.new_value: On the Boa Vista savanna, Sítio Arqueológico da Pedra Pintada rises 35 metres above a cave. Its rock art comes in two styles, the abstract Parime and the realist Surumu.

row.old_value: Circular stone inner wall 3.6 metres thick enclosing a 61-metre space near Sancreed on the Penwith peninsula. The summit commands a 360-degree panorama of the southern Cornish coast.
row.new_value: In Cornwall, the Iron Age hill fort of Caer Bran ringed a space 200 feet in diameter with a stone-lined wall. At its centre lie remains of a large circular stone building.

row.old_value: A pyramid-like Wari mausoleum discovered undisturbed in 2013 with 60 burials, including three elite women. Over 1,000 artifacts were interred with them.
row.new_value: Excavated in secret in 2013 to prevent looting, El Castillo de Huarmey hid a royal Wari tomb: 60 bodies seated in rows, and three royal women buried with gold weaving tools.
